question: In the last few days, Piscinas beach – one of nature’s gems in the south of Sardinia – has taken centre stage in an environmental disaster. The Irvi River, which leads to the beach, has been stained red by the presence of cadmium, lead and zinc: heavy metals from the mining area that closed in 1991.

A number of scientific analyses carried out by the Sardinian environmental protection agency and the National Institute of Health have confirmed the presence of these metals1. The Piscinas area has two sites of Community importance2 supported under Directive 92/43/EEC.

Alarmingly, although the Sardinian authorities have planned clean-up measures and funded a few projects, including some drawing on national development and cohesion funds (FSC), regional operating programme (ROP)* and LIFE funds3, what we are seeing is the steady contamination of the soil and aquifers.

What is more, the dunes on Piscinas beach are protected by a landscape preservation order4 and a blanket conservation order5. Although the various institutions have been saying all the right things, between 2008 and the present day, not a single structural or environmental clean-up project has come to fruition. Given the urgency and the growing threat to health, can the Commission say: 1.
Is it aware of the environmental disaster that has been unfolding in the Piscinas area for the past 30 years?
Could the unchecked release of contaminated waters into the waterways and the sea constitute a serious breach of EU legislation?
Will it disclose what action provided for by EU law it might take against the relevant national and regional authorities?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.6.2024) 1. The Commission does not have detailed information on the matter but received a copy of a letter from a non-governmental organisation asking the Italian authorities to provide information on the pollution of the Piscinas-Irvi river and to take appropriate measures to remedy the situation. 2.

Under the Water Framework Directive1, Member States had to take all measures necessary to bring surface water bodies (including coastal water bodies) to good ecological status or potential and to good chemical status by 2015.

Member States can apply exemptions until 2027, subject to sound justification in their River Basin Management Plans (RBMP), established every six years, setting out the status of water bodies and the measures required to achieve good status.

According to a preliminary analysis of the third RBMP, some water bodies in this area appear to be in poor chemical status, but some measures for the remediation of contaminated sites are planned by the Region of Sardinia. The Commission is assessing the RBMPs for 2021–2027.

It will publish a report including recommendations for each Member State by the end of 2024 and decide in due course on the appropriate action to be taken. 3. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including verifying individual cases of potential breach of the relevant rules.
In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action2 the Commission focuses on systemic non-compliance.
1 Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2000 establishing a

framework for Community action in the field of water policy, OJ L 327, 22.12.2000, p. 1–73, as amended by Commission Directive 2014/101/EU of 30 October 2014, OJ L 311, 31.10.2014, p. 32–35. 2 As set out in the Communication of 19 January 2017: EU law: Better results through better application C/2016/8600, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20 and in the Communication of 13 October 2022: COM(2022) 518 final - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers.
